# Part 1: rapid recap 🚀 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## How this part works

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 30px;"}
- I will name a [concept]{.alert} from one of the seven lectures
- One of you explains it in [your own words]{.alert} (about 30 seconds)
- The rest of us [push back, add nuance, or correct]{.alert}
- I will keep it moving. Wrong answers are useful; silence is not
- We have about 12 minutes for this section
:::

## Concept 1: hallucination

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 32px;"}
- Volunteer or victim? 🙋
- In one sentence: [what is an AI hallucination, and why does it happen?]{.alert}
- Follow-ups for the room:
  - Is a hallucination the same as a [lie]{.alert}?
  - Is a hallucination the same as a [factual error]{.alert}?
  - Why might an open-laptop quiz [punish]{.alert} someone who copy-pastes an LLM answer?
:::

::: {.notes}
Aim for: hallucination = output that is fluent and confident but not grounded in
the training data or the prompt. Different from a "lie" because there is no
intent. Different from a "factual error" because the model often invents
plausible-sounding details. Push the third question to remind students that
verifying sources matters.
:::

## Concept 2: dataset and labels

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 30px;"}
- Pick someone new
- [What does it mean to "label" a dataset, and why is it usually the most
  expensive step?]{.alert}
- Quick room poll: in each case, [is the label easy, hard, or contested?]{.alert}
  - "Is this email spam?"
  - "Is this tweet toxic?"
  - "Is this CT scan showing pneumonia?"
  - "Is this résumé a good fit for the role?"
- Connect to: [garbage in, garbage out]{.alert}
:::

## Concept 3: the three learning paradigms

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- Three students, one paradigm each. One sentence per person:
  - [Supervised learning]{.alert} — ?
  - [Unsupervised learning]{.alert} — ?
  - [Reinforcement learning]{.alert} — ?
- Then back to the room: name one [real product]{.alert} that uses each
- Trick question: where does [training a chatbot with thumbs up / thumbs down]{.alert}
  fit? (answer: RL from human feedback — RLHF)
:::

## Concept 4: precision vs recall

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- This is the single most quiz-worthy concept of the block. 🎯
- Volunteer to [draw the confusion matrix]{.alert} on the board (or describe it)
- Then the room debates:
  - A [cancer screening]{.alert} model — should you optimise precision or recall? Why?
  - A [spam filter]{.alert} for your inbox — same question
  - A [criminal sentencing]{.alert} risk score — same question
- Punchline: the answer depends on [which mistake is more costly]{.alert}, and
  who pays the cost
:::

## Concept 5: overfitting and validation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- Cold call: [what is overfitting, in plain English?]{.alert}
- Follow-up: [why do we split data into training and validation sets?]{.alert}
- Room scenario:
  - You train a model on Emory student grades from 2018-2024
  - It scores 99% accuracy on those students
  - Should you trust it on the 2026 cohort? [Why or why not?]{.alert}
- Connect to: [Goodhart's law]{.alert} — when a measure becomes a target, it
  ceases to be a good measure
:::

## Concept 6: tokens and embeddings

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- Pair up with the person next to you. One minute. 🗣️
  - One of you explains [tokenisation]{.alert}
  - The other explains [embeddings]{.alert}
- Then I pick two pairs to share
- Rapid-fire room questions:
  - Why does ChatGPT charge by the [token]{.alert} and not by the word?
  - Why does the [order]{.alert} of words in a sentence matter, even after
    embedding?
  - What is a [context window]{.alert}, and why does it cost so much to make it
    bigger?
:::

## Concept 7: multimodal

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- Last concept of the recap
- [What does "multimodal" mean for an AI system?]{.alert}
- Room:
  - Name three [modalities]{.alert} we discussed
  - Why is [audio]{.alert} harder than text in some ways and easier in others?
  - When you upload a photo to ChatGPT, what is happening [under the hood]{.alert}?
:::

# Part 2: a real scenario 🏥 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## The setup

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=60%}
A startup, [HealthScribe]{.alert}, sells an AI tool to hospitals. The tool
listens to doctor-patient conversations and writes the clinical note.

- The model is a [fine-tuned LLM]{.alert}
- Training data: 80,000 doctor-patient transcripts from a single large hospital
  network in California, 2019-2024
- The labels are the [final clinical notes]{.alert} that doctors wrote and
  signed off on
- HealthScribe reports [92% agreement]{.alert} with doctor-written notes on a
  held-out test set
- They are now selling the product to hospitals across the country
:::

:::{.column width=40%}
:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
🩺

We will work through this together.

I will [not move on]{.alert} until I get answers from at least three different
people on each question.
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Question A: the dataset

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- [What problems can you spot]{.alert} with the training data?
- Hints, if the room is quiet:
  - Where did the data come from? Who is in it? Who is [not]{.alert} in it?
  - The labels are [doctor-written notes]{.alert} — is that the truth, or one
    person's interpretation?
  - The data is from [2019-2024]{.alert} — does medicine change over five years?
- Try to name [at least three distinct issues]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
Issues to surface: representativeness (one network, one state, one country);
selection (only patients who came to that network); label quality (doctor's
interpretation, not ground truth); temporal drift (medicine evolves, COVID is
in this data); demographic skew (California population is not the US
population); language (probably English-only).
:::

## Question B: the metric

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- HealthScribe reports [92% agreement with doctor-written notes]{.alert}
- Volunteer: [what is being measured here?]{.alert}
- Then the room:
  - Is "agreement with the doctor" the same as [getting it right]{.alert}?
  - What are the model and the doctor [agreeing on]{.alert} when they agree?
  - On what kind of patient might the [8% disagreement]{.alert} concentrate?
- This is a classic case of [Goodhart's law]{.alert}: optimising agreement is
  not the same as optimising care
:::

## Question C: precision and recall

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- Imagine the AI's job is to [flag every mention of an allergy]{.alert} in the
  conversation, so it can be added to the patient record
- The room decides:
  - Would you optimise [precision]{.alert} (only flag what you are very sure of)
    or [recall]{.alert} (flag everything that might be an allergy)?
  - Defend your choice with [a real harm]{.alert} that comes from each kind of
    mistake
- This is the single most likely structure for a quiz question. ✏️
:::

## Question D: a deployment decision

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- Your hospital is considering buying HealthScribe
- The room votes by show of hands:
  - [Yes, buy it]{.alert}
  - [No, do not buy it]{.alert}
  - [Buy it, but with conditions]{.alert}
- Whatever the room votes, I want one defender of each position to [argue for
  60 seconds]{.alert}
- Then the room: [what evidence would change your mind?]{.alert}
:::

# Part 3: practice questions 📝 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## How this part works

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- I will show you [three practice questions]{.alert}, one at a time
- They are written in the same style as the real Quiz 01
- Pair up with the person next to you
- You have [two minutes per question]{.alert} to discuss your answer
- Then I will pick a pair to share, and the room critiques
- These are [not the real quiz questions]{.alert}, but the format is identical
:::

## Practice question 1

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 26px;"}
A friend tells you: "ChatGPT is just an autocomplete on steroids. It doesn't
actually understand anything." Another friend says: "It got 90% on the bar
exam, so clearly it understands law." 🤷

[Your task:]{.alert} who is closer to the truth, and why? In your answer:

1. Explain what [tokenisation and next-token prediction]{.alert} have to do
   with the first friend's claim
2. Explain why [a high benchmark score]{.alert} is not the same as
   understanding (cite Goodhart's law if you can)
3. Take a position. Defend it in 3-4 sentences

[Two minutes. Discuss with your partner.]{.alert} ⏱️
:::

## Practice question 2

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 26px;"}
A university wants to build an AI that flags students who are "at risk of
dropping out." They have:

- Five years of student records (grades, attendance, financial aid status)
- The label is "did this student drop out by the end of year 2"

[Your task:]{.alert}

1. What [kind of learning problem]{.alert} is this (supervised, unsupervised,
   reinforcement)?
2. What is the difference between [precision and recall]{.alert} for this
   model, and which would you optimise? Defend your choice
3. Name [one ethical concern]{.alert} that does not appear anywhere in the
   technical metric

[Two minutes.]{.alert} ⏱️
:::

## Practice question 3

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 26px;"}
You upload a photo of a handwritten recipe to ChatGPT and ask it to convert it
to a typed shopping list. It gets the recipe mostly right, but lists "2 cups
of sugar" when the recipe clearly says "2 cups of salt." 🧂

[Your task:]{.alert}

1. What is happening at the [tokeniser and vision encoder]{.alert} stage that
   could cause this kind of mistake?
2. Is this a [hallucination]{.alert}, a [factual error]{.alert}, or both?
   Explain
3. If you were Anthropic or OpenAI, [what is one thing you would change]{.alert}
   to make this kind of error less likely?

[Two minutes.]{.alert} ⏱️
:::
